summary: Describes how to identify the authoritative server for RDAP queries that are not for domains, addresses or AS numbers, such as entity queries. It is a Best Current Practice.

eli5.summary: Looking up a person or group needs the right office. This adds name tags so you know which office to ask.

questions: how does an rdap client find the authoritative server for an entity
what is a service provider tag in rdap
subtitle: A hyphen and a short provider tag on the end of an RDAP handle tell clients which server to ask.

tldr.problem: RDAP can find the authoritative server for domain name, IP address and AS number queries, but not for entity queries, because entity handles have no structure that points to a provider.
tldr.mechanism: Providers append a tag made of a hyphen and an IANA-registered provider identifier to each handle, such as XXXX-ARIN. A client splits off the part after the last hyphen and looks it up in an IANA bootstrap registry to get the base RDAP URL.
tldr.outcome: Entity queries (and other unstructured identifiers) can now be bootstrapped to the right server. Responses that use the practice must say so with the rdapConformance value rdap_objectTag_level_0.

today: RFC 8521 is a Best Current Practice and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC. It updates RFC 7484.

sections.title: The Bootstrapping Gap in RDAP
sections.content:
The Registration Data Access Protocol (RDAP) has a method, defined in RFC 7484, for finding the authoritative server that should answer a query. It works for domain names, IP addresses and Autonomous System Numbers (ASNs), because each of these is structured so that it can be tied to one service provider. A domain name, for example, has labels such as com, net and org that belong to specific providers.

The same RFC notes that the method does not cover entity queries, name server queries, help queries or queries using certain search patterns. The identifiers behind those queries are typically unstructured, so nothing in them points to a provider.

RFC 8521 is a Best Current Practice that updates RFC 7484. It describes an operational practice that adds structure to RDAP identifiers so that the authoritative server can be found for these additional queries.
sections.eli5: Some lookups, like finding a person's record, do not say which office keeps it. This document adds a label so you know which office to ask.

sections.title: Tagging Object Identifiers
sections.content:
A service provider tag is built by putting the HYPHEN-MINUS character HYPHEN-MINUS (U+002D) in front of an IANA-registered value that stands for the provider. A provider identified as ARIN therefore has the tag -ARIN. The tag is added to the end of an RDAP object identifier, so a handle XXXX at that provider becomes XXXX-ARIN.

Implementing the practice means tagging the unstructured identifiers that appear in RDAP responses. The RFC shows elided response examples in which the handle of a domain, an entity, a nameserver and an IP network carry tags such as -RIR, -DNR and -ABC.

Responses can also contain self links. The tag and the self reference SHOULD be consistent. If they are not, the service provider tag is processed with higher priority when identifying the provider.
sections.eli5: The provider's short name is glued onto the end of each ID with a dash, like a name tag that says KID-SCHOOLNAME.

sections.title: How a Client Finds the Server
sections.content:
A client that wants to bootstrap an entity query splits the tagged identifier into a handle and a provider identifier. Handles can themselves contain hyphens, so the provider identifier is whatever follows the last hyphen.

The client then looks the provider identifier up in an IANA registry to get a base RDAP URL. In the RFC's example, XXXX-YYYY splits into handle XXXX and provider YYYY. The registry maps YYYY to https://example.com/rdap/, and the client forms the query URL https://example.com/rdap/entity/XXXX-YYYY using the entity path segment from RFC 7482.

The client sends the full tagged handle to the provider. Only the lookup in the IANA registry uses the part after the last hyphen.
sections.eli5: You read the school name after the last dash, look it up in a big phone book, and call that school's number to ask about the kid.

sections.title: Why the Hyphen-Minus
sections.content:
There is a risk if a hyphen appears in a handle for some purpose other than separating the tag. A client could wrongly treat it as a separator and look up the text after it as a provider identifier. It would likely get an unexpected, invalid result from the IANA registry. For this reason, any use of the hyphen as a provider tag separator MUST be noted with an rdapConformance value.

The RFC gives two reasons for choosing the hyphen: it is a familiar separator in operational use, and it avoids collision with URI-reserved characters. It considered the unreserved characters from RFC 3986 (letters, digits, and the characters hyphen, full stop, underscore and tilde). Letters and digits were excluded because they are commonly used in handles for non-separator purposes. The remaining characters were excluded because they are not broadly used as separators in entity handles.
sections.eli5: A dash is the character people already use to split names, and it does not clash with the special characters that web addresses use, so it was the best pick.

sections.title: The IANA Bootstrap Registry
sections.content:
IANA created a bootstrap service registry for provider object tags and makes it available as a JSON object. It uses the structure from RFC 7484. Each entry holds a contact email address, an alphanumeric provider identifier and one or more base RDAP URLs. The URLs are expected to supply the same data, though they can differ in scheme or other components.

Provider identifiers match the suffix portion (\w{1,8}) of the roidType syntax in RFC 5730. The registry is filled using the First Come First Served policy from RFC 8126. A request gives an email address, the identifier wanted (or asks IANA to assign one) and one or more base RDAP URLs. IANA also registered the extension identifier rdap_objectTag in the RDAP Extensions registry.
sections.eli5: There is a big public phone book run by a trusted office. Each school signs up first-come, first-served and lists its name and phone number.

sections.title: Declaring Conformance
sections.content:
An RDAP response that contains values described in this document MUST say so by including the rdapConformance value rdap_objectTag_level_0. This is how a client learns that a hyphen in a handle is a provider tag separator and not just part of the name.

The RFC's example response lists both rdap_level_0 and rdap_objectTag_level_0.
sections.eli5: The answer carries a sticker saying 'my IDs end with a school tag', so nobody mistakes the dash for part of the name.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The practice uses IANA as a well-known, centrally trusted authority so that users can get RDAP data from an authoritative source. That lowers the risk of sending queries to non-authoritative sources and revealing query information to unintended parties.

Protecting the connection to IANA with TLS 1.2 (RFC 5246) or TLS 1.3 (RFC 8446) lets the server authenticate itself as operated by IANA. It also gives integrity protection for the referral information and confidentiality for privacy. The later RDAP connection works as usual and keeps the security properties described in RFC 7481.
sections.eli5: You get the phone number from a trusted phone book over a private line, so you do not call the wrong office and tell a stranger what you wanted to know.
